source_text:
Στίχ. β΄. Γυνὴ ἥτις ἐὰν σπερματισθῇ, καὶ τέκῃ ἄρσεν.
Παρέλκειν δόξει τὸ, ἐὰν σπερματισθῇ, προτασσόμενον τοῦ· καὶ τέκῃ ἄρσεν. Ἀλλʼ ἐφίστημι μήποτε ἵνα προφητικῶς ἡ Μαρία, οὐκ ἐκ τοῦ ἐσπερματίσθαι (17) τεκοῦσα ἄρσεν, μὴ νομισθῇ ἀκάθαρτος εἶναι, γεγεννηκυῖα τὸν Σωτῆρα, εἴρηκεν ὅλον Ἐδύνατο δὲ καὶ μὴ προκειμένου τοῦ, Ἐὰν σπερματισθῇ, νοεῖσθαι μὴ οὖσα ἀκάθαρτος ἡ Μαρία· οὐ γὰρ ἀπλῶς γυνὴ, ἀλλὰ παρθένος.
thought_title: Mary's purification and the prophetic wording of the law
orientation: Origen is commenting on Leviticus 12:2, the law about a woman who bears a male child, and argues that its wording prophetically safeguards Mary from being thought unclean.
pass_a_gloss: Verse 2: A woman, whoever is inseminated, and bears a male child. The phrase 'if she is inseminated' will seem to be redundant, being placed before 'and bears a male child.' But I am considering whether perhaps, in order that prophetically Mary, having borne a male child not from being inseminated, might not be thought to be unclean, having given birth to the Savior, it said the whole thing. But it was also possible, even without 'if she is inseminated' being set before, for Mary to be understood as not being unclean; for she was not simply a woman, but a virgin.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'is inseminated' for σπερματισθῇ, and the conditional force of ἐὰν must be kept.
Παρέλκειν means to be superfluous or redundant; δόξει keeps the future tense of 'will seem.'
Ἐφίστημι with μήποτε introduces a cautious deliberative question; 'I am considering whether perhaps' preserves the tentative, exploratory tone.

choices.term: οὐκ ἐκ τοῦ ἐσπερματίσθαι τεκοῦσα ἄρσεν
choices.english: having borne a male child not from being inseminated
choices.why: The participial phrase τεκοῦσα ἄρσεν is modified by the negated prepositional phrase; the word order keeps the negation attached to the means of conception.
rejected: who bore a male without insemination
having given birth to a male not by insemination

choices.term: οὐ γὰρ ἀπλῶς γυνὴ, ἀλλὰ παρθένος
choices.english: for she was not simply a woman, but a virgin
choices.why: Ἀπλῶς means 'simply' or 'merely'; the contrast with ἀλλὰ παρθένος is essential to Origen's argument.
rejected: for she was not just a woman, but a virgin
for she was not merely a woman, but a virgin

bible_refs.note: Γυνὴ ἥτις ἐὰν σπερματισθῇ, καὶ τέκῃ ἄρσεν

pass_b_english: Verse 2: “A woman who, if she is inseminated, bears a male child” (Leviticus 12:2). The phrase “if she is inseminated,” placed before “and bears a male child,” will seem to be redundant. But I am considering whether perhaps it was said for this reason: so that prophetically Mary, having borne a male child not from being inseminated, might not be thought unclean after giving birth to the Savior. Even without the phrase “if she is inseminated” being set down, Mary could be understood not to be unclean, for she was not simply a woman, but a virgin.
